title: AQA GCSE Physics · Energy Changes in a System

items.stem: In physics, what is meant by a system?

options.text: An object, or a group of objects, being studied.
A machine that has been built to move energy.
A group of two or more objects, never one.
A place where energy is kept until used.

items.why: This is the specification's definition: a system is an object or group of objects.

items.stem: What always happens when a system changes?

options.text: Some of the energy in the system is used up.
The way energy is stored in the system changes.
The amount of energy in the system rises.
Extra energy is created inside the system itself.

items.why: This is exactly what the specification says happens when a system changes.

items.stem: Which of these is a way of storing energy rather than a way of transferring it?

options.text: The heating of a large beaker of cold water.
The work done by a steady pushing force.
The elastic store of a squashed spring.
An electric current in a copper wire.

items.why: A stretched or squashed spring holds energy, so this is a store.

items.stem: The specification asks for all the changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. What must such a description name?

options.text: Only the store that empties during the change.
Only the useful store that fills in the change.
The size of the force that is acting on the system.
Each store that empties and each that fills.

items.why: 'All the changes' means both ends of every transfer are named.

items.stem: A ball is thrown straight upwards. As it rises, what happens to the way energy is stored?

options.text: The gravitational store empties, the kinetic store fills.
The kinetic store empties and the gravitational store fills.
The kinetic store keeps filling while the ball rises.
Both the kinetic and the gravitational stores fill.

items.why: The ball slows as it gains height, so the kinetic store empties into the gravitational store.

items.stem: Air resistance is ignored. At the highest point of a ball's flight, what has happened to the energy that was in its kinetic store?

options.text: It was destroyed at the moment the ball stopped.
It has been transferred to the elastic store of the air.
Some remains, because the ball is still moving up.
It has all been transferred to the gravitational store.

items.why: With no air resistance the whole of the kinetic store fills the gravitational store.

items.stem: A trolley moving along a bench hits a wall and stops. What happens to the energy in its kinetic store?

options.text: It is transferred to thermal stores and by sound.
It is destroyed by the impact of the trolley on the wall.
It is used up in bringing the trolley to a stop.
It stays in the kinetic store of the stopped trolley.

items.why: The trolley, the wall and the surrounding air warm slightly and a sound wave carries some energy away.

items.stem: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a smooth, level floor. Which store fills as the box speeds up?

options.text: The gravitational store of the moving box.
The chemical store of the pushing force.
The kinetic store of the moving box.
The elastic store of the smooth floor.

items.why: Work done by the force transfers energy to the kinetic store as the box speeds up.

items.stem: A car slows down when the driver brakes. Which statement describes the changes in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The kinetic store empties into the chemical store of the brakes.
Energy is lost from the car, so the total energy falls.
The kinetic store empties and the thermal stores of the brakes fill.
The kinetic store of the car fills as it keeps moving.

items.why: Friction at the brakes does work, filling thermal stores of the brakes, tyres, road and air.

items.stem: A cyclist stops pedalling on level ground and slowly freewheels to a stop. Which store empties?

options.text: The kinetic store of the cyclist and the bicycle.
The chemical store held in the cyclist's leg muscles.
The gravitational store of the moving bicycle.
No store keeps it, the energy is lost to the surroundings.

items.why: Friction and air resistance do work, emptying the kinetic store into thermal stores.

items.stem: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which statement describes the main change in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The chemical store of the kettle itself empties into the water.
The water gains a store of electrical energy as it is heated.
The kinetic store of the water fills as the water boils.
The current does work and the water's thermal store fills.

items.why: A current in the element does work; the thermal stores of the element and then the water fill.

items.stem: As well as the water, which other thermal stores fill while a kettle boils?

options.text: Only the water's store; nothing else becomes warm.
Those of the kettle and of the air around it.
None, because the water uses up all the energy.
Those of the mains cable and the power supply.

items.why: The element, the kettle body and the surrounding air all end up warmer.

items.stem: 0.50 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, what is the change in thermal energy?
A heater is switched on under a beaker of water. What does heating the water do?

options.text: It raises its temperature but transfers no energy.
It fills the kinetic store of the beaker.
It transfers energy to the water's thermal store.
It uses up energy inside the water each second.

items.why: Heating is a transfer route, and the store it fills is the thermal store of the water.

items.stem: A constant force of 40 N pushes a crate 2.5 m across a floor, in the direction of the force. Using W = F s, how much work is done?
A constant resultant force does work on an object moving horizontally along the line of the force. What does this work do?

options.text: It fills the kinetic store of the object.
It is stored as force inside the moving object.
It uses up the energy the object already has.
It makes the object rise as its kinetic store fills.

items.why: Work done by a resultant force along the motion transfers energy to the kinetic store.

items.stem: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 90 s. Using P = E / t, how much energy is transferred by the current?
items.why: P = E / t rearranges to E = P t, so E = 2000 × 90 = 180 000 J.

items.stem: A current flows through the heating element of a hairdryer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The element holds a store of electrical energy inside itself.
The current is used up as it passes through the element.
The current does work, filling the element's thermal store.
The chemical store of the metal wire empties into it.

items.why: Work done when a current flows is the transfer route; the thermal store fills.

items.stem: An energy diagram drawn to a common scale shows the stores in a system before and after a change. What must be true of the bars?

options.text: The total after the change must be smaller than before.
Every bar after the change matches a bar before it.
The useful output bar must equal the input bar.
The bars after the change add to the same total.

items.why: A common scale shows the same total redistributed between different stores.

items.stem: A lamp is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 60 J to the surroundings by light. Drawn on a common scale, what must the remaining bar show?

options.text: 560 J, the two amounts added together.
440 J, going to thermal stores.
60 J, the same as the light output.
Nothing, the energy has been used up.

items.why: 500 − 60 = 440 J, which fills thermal stores of the lamp and the surroundings.

items.stem: A ball of mass 500 g is moving at a speed of 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.text: 9 J

items.stem: A toy car of mass 0.8 kg is moving at a speed of 5 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.text: 2 J

items.stem: A van doubles its speed. Its mass does not change. What happens to its kinetic energy?

options.text: it grows in the same ratio as the speed
it becomes four times as large as before
it becomes twice as large as before
it stays the same size as before

items.why: Speed is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2, so a factor of 2 on the speed gives a factor of 2^2 = 4 on the energy.

items.stem: Which of these is the equation E_k = 1/2 m v^2 written out in words?

options.text: kinetic energy = 0.5 × (mass)^2 × (speed)
kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed
kinetic energy = mass × (speed)^2
kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2

items.why: This is the equation as the specification states it: the speed, and only the speed, is squared.

items.stem: A kinetic energy calculation uses a mass in kilograms and a speed in metres per second. The answer is in which unit?

options.text: newtons, N
watts, W
joules, J
kg m/s

items.why: Kinetic energy, like every energy store in this section, is measured in joules, J.

items.stem: A student puts the mass of a 250 g ball straight into E_k = 1/2 m v^2 as 250. Why is the answer wrong?

options.text: the speed should not have been squared
the mass has to be in newtons, so m should be 2.5
the answer is right, but the unit is newtons
the mass has to be in kilograms, so m should be 0.25

items.why: The equation needs the mass in kilograms, and 250 g = 250/1000 = 0.25 kg.

items.stem: A car's speed is given as 72 km/h. What must be done before using E_k = 1/2 m v^2?

options.text: convert the speed to metres per second
convert the speed into kilometres per minute
use 72 as the speed and convert the answer
square 72 first and then halve the answer

items.why: The equation requires the speed v in m/s, so 72 km/h must be converted to 20 m/s first.

items.stem: Which pair of quantities is needed to calculate the kinetic energy of a moving object?

options.text: the force applied and the speed reached
the weight and the speed of the object
the mass and the speed of the object
the mass and the distance travelled

items.why: E_k = 1/2 m v^2 contains only the mass and the speed; nothing else about the object is needed.

items.stem: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched, within its limit of proportionality, so that its extension is 0.1 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?

options.text: 1 J

items.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 400 N/m is stretched by an extension of 5 cm, staying within its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

options.text: 1 J

items.stem: The energy stored in a stretched spring is E_e = 1/2 k e^2. What do the symbols k and e stand for?

options.text: the spring constant and the energy of the spring
the spring constant and the force applied to it
the spring constant and the stretched length
the spring constant and the extension of the spring

items.why: k is the spring constant, in N/m, and e is the extension, in m.

items.stem: A spring is stretched within its limit of proportionality. The elastic potential energy stored in it is measured in which unit?

options.text: newtons, N
joules, J
watts, W
N/kg, newtons per kilogram

items.why: Elastic potential energy, like every energy store, is measured in joules, J.

items.stem: In the equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2, the spring constant k is measured in which unit?

options.text: newtons times metres, N m
newtons per kilogram, N/kg
newtons per centimetre, N/cm
newtons per metre, N/m

items.why: The spring constant is the force needed for each metre of extension, so it is measured in N/m.

items.stem: A spring of unstretched length 0.20 m is stretched to a length of 0.26 m. Which length is the extension e used in E_e = 1/2 k e^2?

options.text: the whole stretched length, in metres
the increase in length, in metres
the length before stretching, in metres
the extra length, in centimetres

items.why: The extension is 0.26 - 0.20 = 0.06 m, and the equation needs it in metres.

items.stem: A spring is stretched so far that its limit of proportionality has been exceeded. What does this mean for E_e = 1/2 k e^2?

options.text: the equation still works if e is measured again
the spring constant doubles from that point on
the equation can no longer be used to find the energy
the stored energy still rises with e squared

items.why: The specification states the equation assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded, so beyond that limit it does not apply.

items.stem: Which two quantities must be known to calculate the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring?

options.text: the spring constant and the extension
the spring constant and the force used
the mass of the spring and its extension
the spring constant and the length

items.why: E_e = 1/2 k e^2 needs only the spring constant k, in N/m, and the extension e, in m.

items.stem: A book of mass 800 g is lifted through a height of 1.5 m. The gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. How much gravitational potential energy does the book gain?

options.text: 6 J

items.stem: A box is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp and ends up 2.0 m above the ground. Which value is used as h in E_p = m g h?

options.text: 5.0 m, the distance moved along the ramp surface
3.0 m, the difference in the two distances
2.0 m, the vertical height risen above the ground
7.0 m, the two distances added together

items.why: h is the vertical height gained, and the path taken up the ramp does not change it.

items.stem: Which of these is g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height written in symbols, with the correct unit?

options.text: E_p = 1/2 m g h, giving E_p in joules
E_p = m g h, giving E_p in joules
E_p = m g h, giving E_p in watts
E_p = m h, giving E_p in joules

items.why: This is the equation as the specification states it, and Ep is measured in joules, J.

items.stem: In E_p = m g h, what is g and where does its value come from?

options.text: field strength in N/kg, which must be recalled
field strength in N, given in the exam question
the force of gravity in N, given in the question
field strength in N/kg, given in the question

items.why: Gravitational field strength is measured in newtons per kilogram, and the specification states that its value will be given.

items.stem: Which statement gives the specification's definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?

options.text: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of the whole sample by one degree Celsius.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
The thermal energy stored by one kilogram of the substance at a temperature of one degree Celsius.
The rise in temperature produced when one kilogram of the substance is supplied with one joule.

items.why: The specification's definition: the energy required, for one kilogram of the substance, for a rise of one degree Celsius.

items.stem: Which word equation does the specification give for the energy change when a system's temperature changes?

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ change in temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × final temperature
change in thermal energy = specific heat capacity × temperature change

items.why: The specification's wording exactly: all three quantities are multiplied together.

items.stem: A beaker holds 300 g of water at 80 °C. The water is heated until it reaches 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy of the water?
items.why: 0.300 kg × 4200 J/kg °C × 20 °C = 25 200 J, with the mass converted to kilograms and ∆θ found by subtraction.

items.stem: Water is heated from 18 °C to 78 °C. Which value should be used for ∆θ in ∆E = m c ∆θ, and why?

options.text: 78 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature that the water reaches.
351 K, because temperatures must be converted into kelvin first.
60 °C, because ∆θ means the change in the temperature.
18 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature the water starts at.

items.why: ∆ means 'change in', so ∆θ = 78 − 18 = 60 °C, in degrees Celsius as the specification states.

items.stem: A 250 g metal block is heated by an immersion heater. The joulemeter shows that 10 000 J has been transferred and the block's temperature rises by 20 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
items.why: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) = 10 000 ÷ (0.25 × 20) = 2000 J/kg °C, with the mass converted to kilograms.

items.stem: Which line gives the units the specification uses for the quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ?

options.text: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in °C
∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in kelvin
∆E in J, m in kg, c in J per °C, ∆θ in °C
∆E in J, m in g, c in J/g °C, ∆θ in °C

items.why: Exactly the units the specification lists: joules, kilograms, joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, and degrees Celsius.

items.stem: A hot metal block of mass m cools from 90 °C to 30 °C in still air. What does ∆E = m c ∆θ tell you about the block?

options.text: Nothing at all, because the equation applies only while a system is being heated up.
Its temperature has fallen, but the energy stored in the block has not changed at all.
The block's thermal energy store has fallen by m × c × 60, and that energy is released.
The block is now storing a total thermal energy of exactly m × c × 30 joules.

items.why: The specification's equation covers energy released as well as stored, and here ∆θ is 90 − 30 = 60 °C.

items.stem: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?

options.text: Water heats up faster than aluminium does when both are supplied with the same energy.
Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs more energy than warming 1 kg of aluminium.
A kilogram of water always contains more thermal energy than a kilogram of aluminium.
The temperature rise of a substance is not related to the energy supplied to it.

items.why: The definition applied directly: 4200 J per kilogram per degree Celsius against 900 J for the aluminium.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 1, how is the specific heat capacity of the metal block calculated?

options.text: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
By dividing the energy supplied by the temperature rise of the block only.
By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the starting temperature of the block.
By multiplying the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.

items.why: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), which links the decrease of one energy store to the rise in temperature of the block.

items.stem: A student heats a metal block with an immersion heater but does not insulate it. The energy supplied is measured accurately with a joulemeter. What is the effect on the calculated value of the specific heat capacity?

options.text: There is no effect, because all the energy from the heater goes into the block.
It is too low, because the block has gained less energy than the heater supplied.
It is too low, because energy escaping to the room is lost from the total.
It is too high, because some energy warms the room and the temperature rise is smaller.

items.why: ∆θ is on the bottom of c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), so a reduced temperature rise makes the calculated c too large.

items.stem: Which set of measurements is needed to determine the specific heat capacity of the block in this practical?

options.text: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the final temperature.
The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the temperature rise.
The mass of the block, the power of the heater, and the temperature rise.
The energy supplied by the heater and the temperature rise of the block.

items.why: These three quantities are exactly what c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) needs, measured using AT 1 and AT 5 skills.

items.stem: Two identical 1 kg blocks of the same metal are heated. Block X rises by 10 °C and block Y rises by 30 °C. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Block Y has three times the specific heat capacity of X, because it became three times hotter.
Both blocks needed the same energy, because they have the same mass and are the same metal.
Block Y needed three times as much energy as X, because ∆E is proportional to ∆θ.
Block Y now stores three times as much thermal energy in total as block X does.

items.why: With m and c the same for both, ∆E = m c ∆θ makes the energy transferred proportional to the temperature change.

items.stem: Which statement gives the definition of power?

options.text: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done
The total amount of energy that a device transfers
The time that an energy transfer takes to finish
The force that a machine uses to shift a load

items.why: This is the definition in the specification: power is a rate, so an energy and a time are both involved.

items.stem: Which word equation for power is given in the specification?

options.text: power = energy transferred x time
power = time taken / energy transferred
power = energy transferred / the time
power = the work done x time taken

items.why: Matches power = (energy transferred)/(time), written in symbols as P = E/t.

items.stem: In the equation P = E/t, which units should be used for E and for t?

options.text: energy in newtons and time in seconds
energy in joules and time in seconds
energy in watts and time in seconds
energy in joules and time in hours

items.why: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, J, and time, t, in seconds, s.

items.stem: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of:

options.text: 1 joule
60 watts
1 kilowatt
1 watt

items.why: This is the statement in the specification: 1 joule per second is a power of 1 watt.

items.stem: A kettle transfers 360 000 J of energy in 180 s. What is its power?
items.why: P = E/t = 360 000 / 180 = 2000 W, that is 2000 joules transferred every second.

items.stem: A crane does 90 000 J of work in 30 s. What is the power of the crane?
items.why: P = W/t = 90 000 / 30 = 3000 W, using power = (work done)/(time).

items.stem: Two electric motors lift identical loads through the same height. Motor A takes 4 s and motor B takes 10 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Motor A is more powerful, because it must have done extra work on the load
Motor B is more powerful, because it keeps working for a longer time
Both motors have equal power, because the work done on the load is equal
Motor A is more powerful, because it does the same work in a shorter time

items.why: Equal loads through equal heights means equal work done, so the shorter time gives the greater power.

items.stem: A 1500 W heater is switched on for 300 s. How much energy does it transfer?

options.text: 5 J

items.why: Rearranging P = E/t gives E = Pt = 1500 x 300 = 450 000 J.

items.stem: The specification gives the equation P = W/t. What does W stand for in this equation?

options.text: the power in watts, as W is its unit
the work done, measured in newtons
the weight lifted, in newtons
the work done, measured in joules

items.why: The specification pairs work done, W, with joules, J; power is the work done divided by the time.

items.stem: A motor transfers 15 000 J of energy in 2 minutes. What is its power?
items.why: 2 minutes is 120 s, so P = E/t = 15 000 / 120 = 125 W.

items.stem: A lamp transfers 500 J of energy while a pump does 500 J of work. Which statement about the units is correct?

options.text: Both are in joules, because doing work is a way of transferring energy
Work done is in newtons, so the two quantities cannot be compared
Energy transferred is in watts, so only the work is in joules
Energy transferred is in joules but work done is in watts

items.why: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, and work done, W, in joules.

items.stem: Two cranes lift the same load to the same height. Crane X takes 20 s and crane Y takes 50 s. Which quantity is different for the two cranes?

options.text: the work done on the load
the energy passed to the load
the power of the two cranes
the weight of the loads lifted

items.why: The same work done in different times means different rates of transfer, so the powers differ.
